title: What is Sensitivity Analysis?
subtitle: Testing how a valuation result changes when key assumptions change
openingQuestion: A DCF model produces the result 'fair value is 55,000 VND/share' with one specific set of assumptions. Why isn't this number alone enough to make an investment decision?
openingOptions: DCF never needs its assumptions re-checked

Because the DCF result is extremely sensitive to input assumptions (WACC, growth, margins) - a Sensitivity Analysis needs to be run to see how the result changes across a reasonable range of assumptions, rather than trusting a single point estimate
Just trust whatever number the software calculates
This number is always absolutely accurate, no further checking needed
explanation: Sensitivity Analysis: systematically vary one or more key input variables (WACC, growth rate, margins) across a reasonable range, then observe how the valuation result changes. The result is usually presented as a two-dimensional data table or a range, rather than a single point estimate - accurately reflecting the inherent uncertainty of any forecast about the future.

diagram.label: Observe how the valuation result changes

realWorldExample.company: A sensitivity table in an analyst report
realWorldExample.description: Professional equity research reports typically present a two-dimensional sensitivity table: rows are different WACC levels, columns are different long-term growth levels, and each cell in the table is a corresponding target price.

quiz.question: If Sensitivity Analysis shows a company's value ranging from 40,000 VND to 90,000 VND depending on the WACC and growth assumptions, what does this say about the reliability of a single point valuation figure?
options: A wide range proves the stock is being mispriced
The model is wrong and needs to be rebuilt from scratch
The average of the range should be chosen as the final result
A single point figure creates a false sense of certainty
quiz.explanation: This is the single most important lesson of Sensitivity Analysis: no valuation model produces an absolutely 'correct' number - the result always depends on assumptions. Good investors use Sensitivity Analysis to understand the reasonable VALUE RANGE and the DEGREE OF CONFIDENCE in a conclusion, instead of clinging to a single point estimate from one specific set of assumptions.

quiz.question: An investor only looks at the 'base case' result of a DCF model without checking the accompanying sensitivity table. What is the biggest risk of this approach?
options: Not seeing how sensitive the result is to the assumptions
Not knowing whether the business is growing or not
Not being able to compare the business against industry peers
Not being able to calculate the investment's payback period
quiz.explanation: This is exactly the risk of looking at only a single point figure: it creates an illusion of certainty that a financial valuation model never actually has - a sensitivity table is the tool for investors to correctly understand the true 'margin of uncertainty' behind any valuation conclusion.

quiz.question: Which two variables are usually placed on the two axes of a DCF sensitivity table?
options: Revenue and cost of goods sold in the first year
WACC and the perpetual growth rate
Tax rate and the annual dividend payout ratio
Number of forecast years and shares outstanding
quiz.explanation: These are the two assumptions that drive most of the result and are also the hardest to pin down. A two-dimensional table for them is a familiar sight alongside every serious DCF model.

quiz.question: The valuation result ranges from 40,000 VND to 90,000 VND. The current market price is 85,000 VND. What is a reasonable conclusion?
options: There is no margin of safety, since the price sits near the upper end of the range
You should buy since the price still falls within the reasonable valuation range
You should short sell because the price is above the range's average
No conclusion can be drawn without knowing the company's P/E
quiz.explanation: Being within the range doesn't mean it's attractive. At 85,000 VND, almost every optimistic assumption has to be right just to break even - that is the definition of having no margin of safety left.

quiz.question: Why is sensitivity analysis more important for long-horizon models?
options: Because long-horizon models must always include a Terminal Value
Because long-horizon models usually use a lower discount rate
Because historical data further back is harder to collect
Because assumption errors compound across more years
quiz.explanation: A one-percentage-point error in growth is nearly negligible in year two, but compounded over ten years it becomes a large gap - and then Terminal Value multiplies that gap further.

keyTakeaways: Sensitivity Analysis: testing how a valuation result changes when key assumptions change
Results should be presented as a value range, not a single point estimate
A mandatory step for assessing the reliability and limits of any valuation model

practicePrompt.question: After finishing a DCF model that gives an enterprise value of 10,000 billion, the analyst goes on to vary the WACC assumption from 9% to 11% and the growth rate g from 2% to 4%, seeing how the enterprise value changes under each scenario. What is this step called, and why does it matter?
options: This is called Comparable Company Analysis, since multiple valuation scenarios are being compared
Sensitivity Analysis: testing how a valuation result changes when key assumptions change
This is called Precedent Transaction Analysis, since different past deal scenarios are being examined
This step is unnecessary because the initial DCF model was already accurate enough for a final conclusion
practicePrompt.explanation: Sensitivity Analysis: testing how a valuation result changes when key assumptions change. Because DCF (especially Terminal Value) is highly sensitive to WACC and g, results should be presented as a value range across multiple scenarios, not a single, absolutely certain point figure.

summary.keyIdea: Sensitivity Analysis: testing how a valuation result changes when key assumptions change
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a definition to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Results should be presented as a value range, not a single point estimate

application.title: Build a simple sensitivity table yourself
application.message: Using the Terminal Value example from the previous two lessons, try changing WACC from 10% to 11% and g from 3% down to 2%, and see how much the result changes in percentage terms - that is sensitivity analysis.
application.secondary: You'll be surprised how just a 1% change in an assumption can push the result very far off.

sections.text: After finishing a complete DCF model, the most important question isn't 'what is the final number' but 'how does that number change if my assumptions are slightly wrong'. That is the job of sensitivity analysis.

Sensitivity Analysis: systematically vary one or more key input variables (WACC, growth rate, margins) across a reasonable range, then observe how the valuation result changes. The result is usually presented as a two-dimensional data table: rows are different WACC levels, columns are different long-term growth levels, and each cell in the table is a corresponding target price - rather than a single point estimate.
A value range, not a point estimate

If sensitivity analysis shows a company's value ranging from 40,000 VND to 90,000 VND depending on the WACC and growth assumptions, that tells you the valuation is highly sensitive to assumptions. Investors should view a valuation as a reasonable VALUE RANGE with varying levels of confidence, not an absolutely precise number. The biggest risk of looking only at the 'base case' result and skipping the sensitivity table: an apparently attractive result may only hold within a very narrow range of assumptions, creating an illusion of certainty that a financial model never actually has.

items: Present results as a value range, not a single point estimate
A two-dimensional sensitivity table (WACC × growth) is the most common format in analyst reports
A single base-case result easily creates an illusion of certainty that doesn't actually exist
A mandatory step for assessing the reliability of any valuation model

lines: A valuation number without an accompanying sensitivity table is just a guess dressed up in a formula.
